title: The Wife's Lament: opening, manuscript and genre
short: 'I make this song about myself': a 53-line woman's elegy on fol. 115 of the Exeter Book, opening with a formula of lament.
body: The poem is copied on fols 115r-115v of the Exeter Book, between riddles and the homiletic poem Judgment Day I; the title is modern. Giedd wrecan, 'to utter a song, recite a lay', is a formula used in Beowulf and The Seafarer (Mæg ic be me sylfum soðgied wrecan). The speaker, a woman separated from her lord, tells of exile, hostile kin, and a dwelling in an earth-cave under an oak. Like Wulf and Eadwacer it is classed as a Frauenlied, and it is grouped with the Exeter Book elegies. Standard editions are Krapp and Dobbie (1936), Leslie's Three Old English Elegies (1961), Klinck (1992) and Muir; it is in Mitchell and Robinson's Guide.

title: geomorre, minre sylfre: the speaker is female
short: The feminine inflections of geomor 'sad' and min sylf 'my self' identify the speaker as a woman, despite occasional arguments otherwise.
body: Geomorre is the dative singular feminine of geomor, 'sad, mournful'; minre sylfre (genitive feminine) also marks a woman. Rudolph Bambas (JEGP, 1963) argued nevertheless that the speaker is a male retainer mourning his lord in the manner of The Wanderer, which required treating the endings as scribal error. Most scholars reject this, and the female speaker is now the standard view. Sið (l. 2), 'journey, experience, fate', is the key word of the opening: the poem is the story of her sið, and its plural wræcsiþas recurs in ll. 5 and 38.

title: 'new or old, no more than now'
short: She has never suffered miseries, new or old, greater than now: genitives of comparison and an emphatic understatement.
body: Yrmþa (genitive plural of yrmþ 'misery, hardship') depends on hwæt 'what (of)'. Siþþan ic up weox, 'since I grew up', covers her whole life. Niwes oþþe ealdes, 'of new or of old', are genitives qualifying yrmþa. No ma þonne nu, 'never more than now', is concise and emphatic. The phrase claims that her present grief exceeds any past suffering, a typical elegiac superlative.

title: wite wonn: 'I have struggled with torment'
short: Wonn is the past of winnan 'to struggle, fight, suffer': 'always I have struggled with the torment of my exile-journeys'.
body: A means 'always, ever'. Wite, 'punishment, torment, pain', is the word used for the torments of hell. Wonn is the preterite of winnan, 'labour, strive, endure', taking wite as its object. Wræcsiþa, genitive plural of wræcsið 'journey of exile', defines the torment. The line establishes exile as her permanent state, as in The Wanderer and The Seafarer, but unlike those male speakers she cannot travel in search of a new lord.

title: 'over the tumult of the waves'
short: Her lord has left the people across the sea; gelac 'tumult, play' of waves is a stock phrase of the sea poems.
body: Gelac (related to lac 'play, contest, offering') means 'commotion, tossing', and yþa gelac occurs in other poems for the rough sea. Gewat heonan of leodum, 'went away from the people', and ærest 'first' mark the beginning of her troubles. Whether the lord left in exile, on a voyage or in disgrace is not said. The Husband's Message, which some critics have connected with this poem, describes a lord driven over the sea by a feud.

title: uhtcearu: 'care before dawn'
short: Uht is the last part of the night before dawn; uhtcearu is the sleepless anxiety of that hour, here about where her lord is.
body: Bosworth-Toller glosses uhtcearu as 'care that comes in the early morning', citing this line. The word joins the uht motif found throughout Old English elegy: The Wanderer's exile mourns ana uhtna gehwylce, and The Wife's Lament later has on uhtan ana gonge (l. 35). Hwær min leodfruma londes wære, 'where in the land my prince might be', uses londes as a partitive genitive of place and wære in the subjunctive of uncertainty.

title: leodfruma: 'prince of the people'
short: A heroic term for a chieftain: leod 'people' and fruma 'first, chief'. Her husband is a man of rank.
body: Leodfruma means 'patriarch, prince, chieftain'; it is a poetic word used of leaders and of patriarchs in biblical verse. Its use alongside hlaford (l. 6) and frea (l. 33) gives her husband social rank. Some critics see the poem's terms for the husband as deliberately ambiguous between a lord and a spouse, which has supported both the marital and the allegorical readings (the soul or the Church longing for Christ).

title: folgað secan, wineleas wrecca: 'to seek service'
short: She went 'to seek a following (or service)', a friendless exile: a phrase from the male world of retainers.
body: Folgoð means 'retinue, service, office'; folgað secan normally describes a retainer seeking a lord's service. Applied to a woman, it may mean she followed her husband abroad, sought protection, or (in Bambas's view) that the speaker is male. Wineleas wrecca, 'friendless exile', uses the masculine noun wrecca, the standard word for the exile figure. For minre weaþearfe, 'because of my grievous need' (wea 'woe' and þearf 'need'), gives the reason.

title: The kinsmen's secret plot
short: 'That man's kinsmen' plotted in secret to divide the couple, so that they lived most hatefully, far apart in the world.
body: Þæs monnes, 'of that man', refers to her husband, and his magas, 'kinsmen', act þurh dyrne geþoht, 'through secret thought'. Todælden unc, 'might divide us two', uses the dual unc, which recurs through the poem (wit, unc, uncer), stressing the couple as a unit. Gewidost and laðlicost, superlatives meaning 'most widely apart' and 'most hatefully', describe the separation. Mec longade, 'I longed', is impersonal: 'it caused longing in me'. The kinsmen's hostility supplies the poem's only explicit motive for the separation.

title: herheard: 'a dwelling here' or 'a dwelling in a grove'?
short: The manuscript's herheard is unexplained; editors divide it as her eard 'dwelling here' or read hearh-eard 'grove-dwelling'.
body: Het mec hlaford min ... niman: 'my lord commanded me to take ...'. Most editors divide the manuscript's herheard as her heard (with heard for eard, 'dwelling', or for the adjective 'harsh') and translate 'to take up a dwelling here'. Bosworth-Toller's supplement records hearh-eard, 'a dwelling in a grove', from hearg 'grove, heathen sanctuary'. A. N. Doane (Mediaeval Studies, 1966) built on this a reading of the speaker as connected with a heathen grove or shrine. The command to dwell may come from her husband, which implies he banished her.

title: 'a well-matched man', with a murderous mind
short: She found a man fully suited to her, yet ill-fated, sad, concealing his mind and plotting a crime: the poem's most puzzling portrait.
body: Gemæcne, related to gemæcca 'mate, spouse', means 'fitting, well-matched'. The participles that follow describe him as heardsælig 'ill-fated', hygegeomor 'sad of mind', mod miþende 'concealing his mind' and morþor hycgende 'thinking of murder (or crime)'. Most critics take this man as the husband, perhaps disaffected or guilty of the deed that caused his exile. Some argue for a second man, and Stanley Greenfield (1953) read later lines as a curse on the husband. Morþor means 'murder, deadly sin, great wickedness', so the plot is serious. Translators differ over whether the participles explain the husband's later behaviour or his kin's hostility.

title: beotian: 'we vowed'
short: With happy looks the two vowed that nothing but death would part them: beotian is the heroic verb of vowing.
body: Beotian, 'to threaten, vow, promise', belongs to the heroic beot, the warrior's boast before battle; here it is a lovers' promise. Bliþe gebæro, 'with cheerful bearing', returns ironically in l. 44, where it describes the mask the young man must wear over his grief. Nemne deað ana / owiht elles, 'except death alone, anything else', sounds like a marriage promise. Eft is þæt onhworfen, 'now that is reversed': onhweorfan 'to change, turn around' marks the reversal.

anchor: is nu    swa hit no wære
title: A defective line
short: Line 24 lacks part of its first half-line: the text 'it is now as if it never were' has a gap that editors leave or fill.
body: The manuscript gives only is nu before swa hit no wære, and no alliteration links the half-lines, so editors suspect a loss. Some leave the gap, others supply words, but the sense is clear: their friendship (freondscipe uncer, l. 25) is as if it had never been. Students should note that line counts and numbering in the editions follow Krapp and Dobbie even where lines are defective.

title: fæhðu dreogan: 'endure the feud'
short: Far and near she must endure the enmity of her dearly beloved: fæhþu is feud, hostility, often with legal force.
body: Fæhþ (fæhþu) means 'feud, hostility, vengeance', the formal enmity between kin groups that the law sought to manage with wergild. Mines felaleofan, 'of my much-beloved', probably refers to her husband; the feud is either his towards her or one she suffers because of him. Some readers take it as the enmity she endures as a result of her husband's actions. The Husband's Message (l. 19) uses the same word for the feud that drove the lord abroad.

title: the grove and the oak
short: She was made to dwell 'in a grove of the wood, under an oak-tree, in the earth-cave': setting for both natural and sacred readings.
body: Bearu means 'grove', and actreo is 'oak-tree'. The oak and grove have suggested a heathen holy place, as in Doane's reading; for others, they are simply a remote wild spot outside human settlement. Heht mec mon wunian, 'someone (or a man) commanded me to dwell', uses indefinite mon, 'one', which leaves the agent unclear. The repetition of under actreo in l. 36 frames the passage describing her surroundings.

title: eorðscræf, eorðsele: cave or grave?
short: 'Earth-cave', 'earth-hall': a cave, a barrow or a grave. Some critics read the speaker as dead and speaking from the tomb.
body: Eorðscræf, glossed by Bosworth-Toller 'an earth-cavern, a grave', and eorðsele, 'earth-hall', describe her dwelling. A literal underground chamber, perhaps an ancient barrow, is possible. But the grave sense led Elinor Lench (Comitatus, 1970) and others to read her as one of the 'living dead' speaking from a burial place. Others again see the cave as a prison of banishment or as an image of the soul's exile in the world. Eald is þes eorðsele, 'this earth-hall is old', also suggests an ancient grave mound. Eal ic eom oflongad, 'I am wholly seized with longing'.

title: the landscape: dim valleys and briars
short: Dark valleys, high hills, bitter enclosures overgrown with briars, a dwelling without joys: a hostile landscape that mirrors her mind.
body: Dena (plural of denu 'valley') dimme 'dark', and duna uphea 'high hills' form a pair. Burgtunas, 'enclosures, fortified dwellings' (burh 'fort' and tun 'enclosure'), are bitre 'bitter' and brerum beweaxne 'overgrown with briars', a sense of abandoned settlement like that of The Ruin. Wic wynna leas, 'dwelling empty of joys', sums up. The landscape is both physical and emotional, a typical feature of the elegies.

title: fromsiþ frean: 'my lord's departure'
short: 'Very often the departure of my lord seized me cruelly here': fromsið, 'a going away', is the cause of her grief.
body: Fromsið means 'departure, going away'. Frea is 'lord', used both of secular lords and of God, which keeps the allegorical reading open. Begeat 'seized, came upon' (from begietan) takes mec as object, so the departure is an active force that overwhelms her (wraþe 'cruelly'). The line repeats the opening narrative (ærest min hlaford gewat, l. 6), so the departure that began her troubles is still, in memory, happening again and again (ful oft). The juxtaposition with the next sentence, about lovers who lie together, sharpens the sense of absence.

title: lovers in their beds
short: 'There are lovers on earth, living dear ones, who keep their bed': the contrast between other couples and her solitude.
body: Leger means 'a lying, a bed, a couch', but also 'sickness' and 'a grave'. Weardian 'to guard, occupy, keep' gives 'they occupy their bed'. Frynd 'friends' here clearly means 'lovers'. The double sense of leger (bed and grave) supports the living-dead reading, but the main contrast is between others who lie together and the speaker who goes alone (ana gonge) before dawn.

title: 'when I go alone before dawn'
short: Alone at dawn under the oak, she can sit through the summer-long day and weep her exile, never resting from her sorrow.
body: On uhtan, 'before dawn', recalls uhtceare (l. 7). Sumorlangne dæg, 'the summer-long day', is a powerful contrast to the winter imagery of the male elegies; the long day lengthens her weeping. Mot and mæg, 'may, can', express both permission and limitation: she may only sit and weep. Modceare and longaþes, genitives after gerestan 'rest from', conclude the narrative section with 'all the longing that has seized me in this life'.

title: The gnomic ending: maxim or curse?
short: 'Always must a young man be sad of mind': a general maxim, a description of her husband, or a curse on him?
body: The subjunctives (scyle, sy) can be read as general statements ('a young man must always be...') or as wishes ('may he be ...'). If gnomic, the passage describes a man who must maintain a cheerful expression despite grief, which may apply to her husband. If optative, it is a curse: may all his joy depend on himself alone, may he be outlawed far away. Stanley Greenfield (1953) argued for a curse, Barrie Ruth Straus (1981) read the end as a speech act of cursing, and John Niles (2003) distinguished gentle from vindictive readings. Sinsorgna gedreag, 'the crowd of perpetual sorrows' (sin 'continual'), and gelong 'dependent' are key terms.

title: The husband imagined under a rocky slope
short: She pictures her friend sitting under a rock-cliff, frosted by storm, flooded by water, in a dreary hall.
body: Stanhliþ, 'stony slope, cliff', storme behrimed 'rimed with frost by storm', and wætre beflowen 'flowed about by water' create a landscape matching hers. Dreorsele (dreor 'blood' or 'dreary', and sele 'hall') is glossed 'a dreary, desolate-looking hall'. Werigmod, 'weary of mind', fits the elegiac exile. The passage mirrors her own hall of earth; both lovers are alone in a hostile place, whether this is a projection of her imagination or the outcome of the curse.

title: The closing gnome
short: 'Woe is to the one who must wait in longing for a loved one': the poem closes with a general sentence applicable to both lovers.
body: He gemon to oft / wynlicran wic, 'he remembers too often a more joyful dwelling', ties the husband's grief to memory. The last gnome, with of langoþe, 'out of longing', and abidan 'wait for', returns to the key word longaþ. Its generality makes it fit either lover; it can also be read as the speaker's own last word. The closing gnome is a common device in the Exeter Book elegies (compare The Wanderer's last lines).
